name: HLHS

question.stem: A 6-year-old boy with a history of hypoplastic left heart syndrome, status post staged single-ventricle palliation with extracardiac fenestrated Fontan procedure at 3 years of age, presents to his pediatrician for Well Child Check. He is asymptomatic, growing well, and participates in gym class without limitation. His mother asks what testing he will need going forward to monitor for long-term complications of his Fontan physiology.
question.prompt: Which of the following would NOT be appropriate as part of his routine annual monitoring?

explanation.text: Fontan physiology creates a chronic, non-pulsatile, elevated systemic venous pressure state that places multiple organ systems at risk over time. Routine annual laboratory and clinical surveillance is aimed at detecting these systemic complications early, even in asymptomatic patients:

items: A. Serum GGT — appropriate. GGT (along with other liver enzymes) is used to screen for Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD), which results from chronic hepatic venous congestion and can progress silently to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma. GGT elevation is often one of the earliest biochemical clues to hepatic congestion in this population.

B. Serum BUN and creatinine — appropriate. Chronically low cardiac output and elevated systemic venous pressure predispose Fontan patients to renal dysfunction, so renal function is monitored as part of routine annual surveillance.

C. Pulmonary function testing — NOT appropriate as routine annual monitoring. While Fontan physiology is critically dependent on passive, low-resistance pulmonary blood flow (making pulmonary status clinically important, e.g., in the context of plastic bronchitis or restrictive lung disease from prior thoracotomies), routine annual PFTs are not part of standard asymptomatic Fontan surveillance protocols. PFTs are reserved for patients with respiratory symptoms, suspected plastic bronchitis, or declining exercise tolerance — not obtained reflexively every year in a well-appearing child.

D. Tanner staging — appropriate. Growth and pubertal development are monitored annually in all children with chronic cardiac disease, as growth failure and delayed puberty are recognized complications of single-ventricle physiology and chronic low cardiac output.

E. Serum albumin and total protein — appropriate. These screen for protein-losing enteropathy (PLE), a serious Fontan complication caused by lymphatic congestion and enteric protein loss, presenting with hypoalbuminemia, edema, ascites, and effusions.

bottomLine: Annual Fontan surveillance targets the known systemic complications of chronically elevated venous pressure — hepatic (GGT/LFTs), renal (BUN/Cr), enteric/lymphatic (albumin/total protein), and growth/pubertal (Tanner staging) — but pulmonary function testing is not a routine annual screening test and is only pursued when clinically indicated by respiratory symptoms.
